_comment: Authored question content, keyed by the item ids in competency.py.
⚠️ THIS FILE IS THE EXPERT-AUTHORING BOTTLENECK, MADE VISIBLE. The engine handles all 34
items in the bank; this file holds authored content for 8 of them. That is not laziness —
writing a distractor and naming the misconception it encodes is subject-expert work, and it
is the scarce resource in this product, not the AI.
⚠️ `misconceptions` maps each WRONG option to the specific error it encodes. This is
distractor analysis, and it is what makes the tutor not a chatbot: the same question with two
different wrong answers must produce two different explanations, and no language model can do
that from the question alone — it does not know which option the candidate picked.
⚠️ The misconception LABEL is authored by a human and is authoritative. The generated part is

q-001.stem: A search system returns nothing for the query `ERR_AUTH_1180` even though that exact string appears in twelve documents. The system uses dense embeddings only. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The index was not rebuilt after the documents were added
options.B: The embedding model maps the identifier toward its neighbourhood of meaning, so it is not retrievable as a literal
options.C: The query is too short for cosine similarity to be meaningful
options.D: The documents were added with the wrong metadata filter

misconceptions.A: reaches for an operational cause (a stale index) before a representational one, without checking whether the string is in the corpus
misconceptions.C: believes similarity degrades with short queries, when length is not what breaks identifier matching
misconceptions.D: attributes a ranking failure to a filter, when a filter being wrong would exclude whole documents rather than one string

q-002.stem: You want to combine a BM25 ranking with a cosine-similarity ranking. Why is summing the two scores unsafe?

options.A: BM25 scores are unbounded while cosine is bounded to [-1, 1], so the larger-scale scorer dominates and the dominance changes as the corpus grows
options.B: Cosine similarity is negative for unrelated documents, which cancels out the BM25 contribution
options.C: BM25 and cosine measure different things, so their sum has no units
options.D: The two scores are computed over different document sets

misconceptions.B: attributes the problem to a sign cancellation that does not occur, rather than to the difference in scale
misconceptions.C: states a units objection, which is true in spirit but is not the mechanism that makes the sum unsafe in practice
misconceptions.D: assumes the scorers see different candidate sets, when the fusion step is given the same corpus

q-006.stem: A retrieval system always returns its top five passages. For a question the corpus cannot answer, what should it do?

options.A: Return the five closest passages and let the caller judge relevance
options.B: Return an empty list and raise an error, because the question is invalid
options.C: Return an explicit 'not covered' result, because similarity is relative and always produces confident-looking neighbours
options.D: Lower the similarity threshold until at least one passage is returned

misconceptions.A: leaves the sufficiency judgement to a caller who has only the scores — which is the problem, since the scores do not separate answerable from unanswerable
misconceptions.B: treats an unanswerable question as an error, when refusing is the correct answer rather than a failure
misconceptions.D: resolves an abstention by weakening the threshold, which guarantees an answer and therefore guarantees wrong ones

q-008.stem: A 946 KB document is passed to a chunker and the encoder has a 512-token limit. What is the failure mode if the chunker cannot split a single large unit?

options.A: The encoder raises an error and the document is skipped
options.B: The chunk is stored whole and the encoder embeds only the beginning, so the rest is in the index but invisible to retrieval
options.C: The document is split at the token limit automatically by the encoder
options.D: Retrieval works but is slower because chunks are larger

misconceptions.A: expects a loud failure, when the measured behaviour is silent and every evaluation still passes
misconceptions.C: assumes the encoder truncates for you in a way that preserves retrieval, which is the belief that hides the bug
misconceptions.D: expects a performance cost rather than a correctness cost, which is the wrong axis entirely

q-010.stem: You store character offsets for each chunk so a citation can highlight the source text. Which invariant must hold?

options.A: The chunk text must be lexicographically greater than the previous chunk's
options.B: Chunk IDs must be stable across re-indexing
options.C: The chunk text must equal the document slice at its recorded offsets
options.D: The chunk must not contain any newline characters

misconceptions.A: confuses ordering with correspondence — chunks can be ordered correctly and still point at the wrong text
misconceptions.B: addresses index stability, which matters for caching but does not make a citation correct
misconceptions.D: imposes a formatting rule unrelated to whether offsets map back to the source

q-021.stem: Two reviewers agree on 88.9% of their ratings, but one of them gives the same score to every single item. How should this be interpreted?

options.A: The agreement is high, so the rubric is reliable
options.B: The agreement is high but chance-corrected agreement is near zero, so the measurement carries no information
options.C: The constant rater should be dropped and the remaining rater's scores used
options.D: The agreement figure needs a larger sample before it means anything

misconceptions.A: treats raw agreement as a measurement, which is exactly what chance correction exists to prevent
misconceptions.C: removes the rater rather than recognising that agreement was never informative in the first place
misconceptions.D: prescribes more data for a problem that more data will not fix — the agreement is chance agreement at any sample size

q-022.stem: An automated judge agrees with human raters 90% of the time on adjacent scores. What must be checked before using it to gate releases?

options.A: Whether the judge's average score matches the human average
options.B: Whether the judge can detect the specific case that must fail, which is a different measurement from average agreement
options.C: Whether the judge runs fast enough to be used in CI
options.D: Whether the judge's prompt is shorter than the context limit

misconceptions.A: checks calibration, which can be perfect while the judge cannot fail a release that must be failed
misconceptions.C: optimises throughput before establishing that the signal is valid
misconceptions.D: addresses an operational constraint rather than whether the judge is usable at all

q-027.stem: The first search against a newly started service takes 351 seconds and later searches take milliseconds. What is the most likely explanation?

options.A: A cold disk cache, which would resolve after the first few queries
options.B: An in-process index that is built on first use and lives in memory, so the cost is paid again on every restart
options.C: A missing database index, which would make all queries slow rather than only the first
options.D: Connection pool warm-up in the retrieval client

misconceptions.A: explains one slow query but not the recurrence of the cost after every process restart
misconceptions.C: predicts uniform slowness, which contradicts the measurement that later queries are fast
misconceptions.D: attributes a one-off 351-second cost to connection setup, which is orders of magnitude too small
